Last winter I took the first job anyone offered me. I'm Tushar, and I was fifteen and desperate for money for a new cricket bat.

A man I'd never met messaged me after seeing my post in a local group. "Food deliveries on your cycle. Nine to one at night. Cash daily. No papers needed." It sounded easy. I didn't ask who he was, or what the rules were for someone my age. I didn't tell my parents; I said I was studying at Lalremsiami's.

The first night I rode alone through dark lanes near the highway. At midnight two men on a bike followed me for a whole street. I was shaking. The next morning I fell asleep in the first period, and the teacher sent me to the office.

That afternoon I told my father everything. He called the number, told the man I was a minor and wouldn't be coming, and blocked it.

For a week Rafiq came in pale, yawning through first period. On Thursday he put his head on the desk and fell asleep during the test.

I asked him to stay back. After some hesitation, he told me that a man he met at the bus stand had offered him delivery work, carrying parcels on a scooter from 10 pm to 2 am. Cash, no questions. He did not know what was in the parcels. His friend Anirban had warned him, but he had said the money was too good.

I told Rafiq he had done the right thing by telling me and that he was not in trouble with me. I explained that night work of this kind is not allowed for someone his age and could be unsafe. I phoned his mother before he left school that afternoon, and she came in. He has agreed not to return to the job. I have informed the principal.

I'm Hemant, and my neighbour Gargi started selling handmade clay earrings from her balcony this year. At first she charged forty rupees a pair, because, she said, "Nobody will pay more."

She was always tired. I'd see her working at midnight, and she ran out of clay every week.

One evening she sat on the steps with a notebook and a calculator, muttering aloud. "Clay, paint, hooks: twenty-two rupees. One hour per pair. The girl in the next lane charges a hundred and twenty for the same thing." She stared at the page. "So I'm getting eighteen rupees for an hour's work."

The next week, her price card said ninety rupees. She lost two buyers. But she stopped working till midnight, and her mother said she seemed less stressed.

I can't know everything she was thinking. But she looked like she'd found something out.

In Accra, Ada started tutoring one boy in maths after school and earned more in a week than she'd ever had. Her friend Abebe was impressed. "Take more!"

Her chemistry teacher returned a test marked 11 out of 30. Ada stared at it. She'd scored 25 on the last one.

At lunch, Abebe asked, "You okay? You look awful."

But that night, looking at her notes for the three tutoring lessons she hadn't prepared, and her own chemistry homework untouched, she did the maths. The money was good. But she was trading her own grades and sleep for it, and that trade didn't look good at all.

Dear Vijay,

Remember I told you about my Saturday coding classes for kids? It was great till the half-yearly results. My maths went from 78 to 54. That scared me.

So I sat down with Mummy and Papa and did what you once suggested: set a cap. Now it's six hours a week, maximum. Saturday morning and Wednesday evening, and that's it, even if more parents ask.

And the big one: no classes at all in exam months. February, March and September are blocked on the calendar in red. The parents of my students already know.

Papa also made me write one line: "If any test goes below 65, the gig pauses for a month." We all signed it, a bit jokingly.

It's been six weeks. My maths is back to 71. And oddly, I enjoy the classes more now that they don't eat my whole week.

Vaibhav

Kiran felt heat rise in their face. "I'm really sorry. I had exams and I underestimated the painting time."

Mrs. Bora softened a little. "His school sports day is in two weeks."

Kiran wrote a new sign for the corner table that evening: "Custom banners: ready in 5 days." Fewer orders came. None came back angry.

Dear Jeevan,

Something happened with my cake orders that I want to tell you about, because you just started your own thing.

Last Sunday a lady from the next block messaged me: the chocolate cake I'd promised for her daughter's birthday at four arrived at six, and the icing had melted in the heat. She was really upset. I wanted to make excuses: the power cut, the oven, my maths tuition. I didn't. I just said sorry.

Then I offered to bake a fresh one for free the next weekend, and I delivered it an hour early.

What I learned: I'd been promising any time people wanted, because saying "not possible" felt rude. Now I tell people "two days' notice, delivery by noon". Some say no. But the ones who order are happy.

Honestly, her complaint taught me more than all the nice reviews.

Nitin

In Class 11, I was sure my problem was laziness. I'm Tanuja, and I was always behind, always tired, and always telling myself to try harder.

One Sunday my friend Arnab said, "Just add up your week. Actually add it."

So I did, on the back of a physics notebook. School: 36 hours. Three coaching batches: 12 hours. Travel between them on two buses: 7 hours. Homework and coaching assignments: 7 hours. Total: 62 hours. Rest: I searched for it and couldn't find any. Even Sunday mornings had a test series.

I looked at that number for a long time. Sixty-two. A full-time job is less.

It changed how I saw myself. I wasn't lazy. I was overloaded. The question wasn't how to push harder. It was what to cut.

I took the sheet to my parents that evening. That was the start of dropping one batch.

Counsellor's note, Class 11 Science

Hansa came to me because she felt she was "not working hard enough". Her friend Lalremsiami had brought her, saying she cried in the washroom after a test.

Rather than talk about effort, I asked Hansa to list every fixed hour in her week. She wrote: school, 35; coaching, three batches, 13; buses and autos, 8; homework, 6. She added it herself: 62. I asked where rest was. She looked at the sheet for a while and said, "There isn't any."

She was quiet, then said, "So it's not that I'm lazy." I agreed that the list showed load, not lack of effort.

We agreed she would take the sheet home and talk to her parents about which batch helped least. I will meet her next week, and I have asked for a meeting with her parents too.
